title: Business Models of Media
description: Two-sided markets, attention economy, why news is expensive to produce

concepts.title: Why Media Markets Are Different
concepts.contentHtml:
Media businesses share a peculiar economic structure that distinguishes them from most other industries. First-copy costs are high; marginal costs are low. A New York Times investigation may take a team of reporters and editors months and tens of thousands of dollars to produce; reproducing it for one additional reader costs essentially zero. The same applies to a Hollywood film, a Pixar animation, a streaming series, or a video game. Once produced, content is what economists call non-rival — one person's consumption does not diminish another's.

Combined with the fact that information is also partially excludable (you can paywall it, but determined users can usually find ways around) and experience-good-like (you don't fully know what you're getting until you've consumed it), this produces a market structure that rarely settles into the textbook competitive equilibrium. Industries with these features tend toward winner-takes-most distributions, persistent natural-monopoly tendencies, and recurring questions about how production should be funded.

The information-good problem means the social value of media production is hard to capture privately. A piece of investigative journalism that exposes corporate fraud may produce enormous value to society — investors, regulators, future consumers, future shareholders — only a fraction of which can be charged back to the journalism's actual readers. The recurring concern of media economics is what funding mechanisms can sustain socially valuable production when the private value falls short.

concepts.title: Two-Sided Markets and the Attention Economy
concepts.contentHtml:
The dominant 20th-century media business model was the two-sided market: media firms produced content that attracted audiences, then sold those audiences to advertisers. Newspapers, magazines, radio, broadcast television, and most cable networks operated this way. The economist Jean Tirole and his co-author Jean-Charles Rochet developed the formal theory of two-sided markets in the 2000s; their insight, recognised in Tirole's 2014 Nobel Prize in economics, was that prices on each side of such markets are not set independently but interact through the network effects between them.

The two-sided structure has unusual properties. Cross-subsidies are common: media firms charge advertisers more than the advertising costs them to deliver, and use the resulting revenue to subsidise the audience-facing product. The classic free-to-air broadcast network, the free local newspaper, the early internet portal — all operated by treating audience attention as the product they were selling, even when audiences experienced the relationship as receiving something for free.

The attention economy framing, popularised by Herbert Simon in the 1970s and applied to digital media by Tim Wu's The Attention Merchants (2016), generalises this insight. Media firms compete for the scarce resource of human attention; the audiences they assemble are sold to advertisers; the structure recurs across centuries of media technology. What changes are the technologies of attention capture and the granularity of measurement, not the underlying business logic.

concepts.title: Why News Production Is Expensive — and Threatened
concepts.contentHtml:
Within the broader media industry, news production faces particularly harsh economics. A daily newspaper's investigative team, foreign correspondents, statehouse reporters, copy editors, and lawyers represent a fixed-cost structure that requires substantial revenue to sustain. The mid-20th-century American daily newspaper covered these costs through monopoly classified-advertising revenue (which underwrote much of the editorial budget), retail display advertising, and modest subscription fees.

The internet broke each of these revenue streams in turn. Classified advertising migrated to Craigslist, eBay, Indeed, Zillow, and a constellation of vertical-search sites; the dollar value local newspapers had collected for car listings, job ads, and real-estate listings collapsed by an estimated 70–80% over two decades. Display advertising migrated to Google and Meta, who collectively now command roughly 60% of the global digital ad market. Subscriptions survived but at scale much smaller than the print-era reader base.

The result has been a sustained contraction of US local news, with around 2,500 newspapers closing between 2005 and 2022 (more than 3,200 by 2024) and total newsroom employment falling by more than half. The 'news desert' phenomenon — counties with no local news organisation at all — affected over 200 US counties by the mid-2020s. Comparable contraction has occurred in most advanced economies, though the public-service-broadcasting layer in Europe has cushioned the decline. The economic question of how socially-valuable news production can be funded in a post-classified, post-display-monopoly environment is one of the central media-policy questions of the era.

title: Advertising-Funded Media
description: Display, classifieds, broadcast ads — the 20th-century revenue model

concepts.title: The Display-Advertising Era
concepts.contentHtml:
The 20th-century newspaper, magazine, radio, and television industries built around display advertising — full-page ads in the New York Times, half-page magazine spreads, 30-second TV spots, drive-time radio reads. The format priced in two dimensions: reach (how many audience members were exposed) and frequency (how many times the same audience was exposed in a campaign). The standard pricing metric was the CPM — cost per thousand impressions — which allowed comparison across very different media properties.

The economic structure favoured publishers with audience scale. National magazines (Time, Life, Reader's Digest), the broadcast networks, and major metropolitan dailies could charge premium rates because of the audience sizes they assembled. The New York Times's 2024 print circulation, about 300,000, is roughly an eighth of the 2.4 million daily copies the New York Daily News alone delivered in the late 1940s. The mass-circulation magazines — Life folded its weekly run in 1972, Saturday Evening Post in 1969, Look in 1971 — were among the first major casualties of the post-television transformation of advertising.

The creative side of the advertising industry developed alongside its measurement infrastructure. Madison Avenue agencies — JWT, BBDO, Y&R, Ogilvy & Mather, DDB — became cultural institutions in their own right. The 1960s creative revolution under Bill Bernbach at DDB shifted the industry from rational-selling-proposition advertising to creative-led, often ironic ad voices that would dominate the next half-century. Advertising's effect on consumer culture, family life, and political campaigns through the broadcast era was sustained, obvious, and only partly tractable to economic analysis.

concepts.title: Classifieds, Yellow Pages, and Local Information
concepts.contentHtml:
The most consequential single advertising format for newspaper economics was the classified ad. A car for sale, a help-wanted listing, an apartment rental, a yard sale, a personal ad — millions of small text-based listings, each priced at a few dollars and aggregated by a local newspaper that monopolised the local-information market. By the 1980s, classified advertising provided 30–40% of total revenue for typical metropolitan US dailies, and a much higher share for local and community papers.

The classifieds business depended on the newspaper's local-information monopoly. There was nowhere else to advertise a used car if you wanted local buyers to see it; nowhere else to find local job listings if you were looking for work. The newspaper aggregated the entire local market into a single source. The same logic applied to the Yellow Pages — the printed directory of business listings that produced enormous profit margins for telephone companies in the late 20th century.

The internet broke this aggregation. Craigslist (founded 1995, expanded nationally through the early 2000s) handled used cars, apartments, jobs, and personals at zero or low cost. eBay (1995), Monster (1994), Indeed (2004), Zillow (2006), and a constellation of vertical search sites further unbundled the classifieds market. By 2010, US newspaper classified revenue had collapsed by roughly 75% from its peak, and most newspaper businesses were structurally damaged in ways advertising-side recovery could not address.

concepts.title: The Broadcast Ad Market and Its Decline
concepts.contentHtml:
The broadcast advertising market peaked in the late 20th century at scale matched by no other single industry. US television advertising alone was an approximately $70 billion business at its peak in the late 2010s, with the major broadcast networks each commanding millions of dollars per minute for prime-time inventory. The Super Bowl became the iconic single-event advertising market, with 30-second spot prices climbing from around $1 million in the mid-1990s to over $7 million by 2024.

The structure of the market reflected the broadcast-era mass audiences. Upfront advertising — the annual May–June sales process during which networks sold the bulk of next season's inventory in advance — institutionalised the rhythm. Scatter market sales filled in remaining inventory closer to airdate, often at higher CPMs. Make-goods compensated advertisers for ratings shortfalls. The whole apparatus assumed a small number of large network properties commanding most of the available audience attention.

The post-2010 decline of broadcast advertising followed cord-cutting and the digital-platform shift. The combined US TV ad market peaked around 2018 at about $73 billion and has been falling progressively since. The largest single advertisers — automakers, consumer-packaged goods, financial services — increasingly moved spend to digital platforms with better targeting and measurement. The broadcast networks have responded with addressable-television initiatives, ad-supported streaming tiers, and digital extensions, but the structural shift has been substantial. The 20th-century broadcast advertising model has not disappeared, but it has been demoted from dominant to one of several revenue layers that publishers must combine to make their economics work.

title: Subscriptions, Paywalls, Patronage
description: NYT, Substack, Patreon — direct reader funding in the digital era

concepts.title: The Paywall Era
concepts.contentHtml:
For much of the 1995–2010 period, the dominant assumption among newspaper publishers was that online readers would not pay. The 'information wants to be free' ideology of the early web, the difficulty of building paywall infrastructure, and the perceived risk of losing search-engine traffic combined to keep most major news sites free. Most papers tried briefly with hard paywalls in the late 1990s and abandoned them when traffic collapsed.

The transformation came with the metered paywall. The New York Times's March 2011 launch of a paywall that allowed a small number of free articles per month before requiring subscription was the breakthrough. The model preserved most search and social-referred traffic (which converted to free article reads) while monetising the heaviest readers (who were most likely to convert to subscribers). Within a decade the Times had over 9 million digital subscribers; by 2024, over 11 million. The Wall Street Journal's pre-existing harder paywall, the Financial Times's metered approach, and similar implementations at the Washington Post, Guardian (with a voluntary-membership model), and most major regional papers reshaped the industry's revenue mix.

The subscription model works much better for some kinds of journalism than others. National brands with distinctive value propositions (NYT, WSJ, FT, Economist) have built large digital subscriber bases. Local papers without comparable distinctive content, and tabloid-format papers competing on entertainment value, have found subscriptions much harder. The result has been a substantial reshaping of the news ecosystem: a small number of national winners alongside a hollowed-out local-news layer where the subscription model has not produced sustainable economics.

concepts.title: Substack, Patreon, and Direct Patronage
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-2015 emergence of direct-payment platforms created a parallel funding model for individual creators rather than institutional publishers. Patreon (founded 2013 by Jack Conte and Sam Yam) provided subscription infrastructure for any creator: musicians, podcasters, educators, journalists, artists. By 2024 Patreon supported over 250,000 creators with paying patrons.

Substack (founded 2017) combined an email-newsletter platform with subscription-payment infrastructure aimed specifically at writers. The combination produced a successful new layer of independent journalism: writers including Bari Weiss, Andrew Sullivan, Glenn Greenwald, Matt Taibbi, Heather Cox Richardson, and Casey Newton built six-figure subscription businesses. The total Substack writer payouts crossed $300 million by 2024. Smaller competitors such as Beehiiv, Ghost, and Buttondown offered similar capabilities with various commercial twists.

The intellectual model of direct-patronage funding is older than the internet. NPR's pledge drives, Wikipedia's annual fundraising, public broadcasting's underwriting model, the recurring 'reader-funded journalism' experiments at organisations like The Tyee, De Correspondent, and ProPublica all draw on the same logic: bypass the advertising layer, ask the audience directly. The digital-era addition has been the payment infrastructure (Stripe, in particular, has made small recurring payments practical at scale) and the platform aggregation. Whether this model can sustain a sufficiently large slice of the news ecosystem to compensate for the decline of advertising-funded news is one of the central open questions.

concepts.title: Membership, Crowdfunding, and Bundling
concepts.contentHtml:
Several other revenue innovations have emerged alongside subscriptions and patronage. Membership models — pioneered by The Guardian (voluntary support without paywall), NRC Handelsblad, and De Correspondent — combine paywalled or premium content with a relationship-rather-than-transaction framing. The Atlantic, New Yorker, and other publications have introduced membership tiers above standard subscriptions that include events, member-only content, and other benefits. The model emphasises identification with the publication rather than purely instrumental access.

Crowdfunding for individual journalism projects has produced occasional successes, from Andy Baio's projects through to investigative non-profits. The 'long tail' of small magazines and projects funded through Kickstarter campaigns is substantial in aggregate but each project tends to fund a single piece or season rather than ongoing operations. The non-profit news sector — ProPublica, the Marshall Project, Texas Tribune, City Bureau, and an emerging US local-news non-profit network — has grown substantially in the post-2010 period, partly funded by foundation grants and partly by reader contributions.

The bundling model — Apple News+, the Athletic (acquired by NYT 2022), Substack's reader subscription bundles — attempts to recreate the economics of cable bundles in a subscription-news world. The model has had limited success: most bundle products have not achieved the scale needed to fundamentally reshape publisher economics. The fundamental tension is that the publishers most willing to bundle (those with weaker direct-subscriber appeal) reduce the bundle's value, while publishers with strong direct relationships are reluctant to dilute them. The post-cable bundle model for news has not yet been found.

title: Conglomerates & Concentration
description: Murdoch, Disney, Bertelsmann — when ownership consolidates

concepts.title: The Logic of Media Consolidation
concepts.contentHtml:
Media industries have a strong tendency toward horizontal consolidation — multiple newspapers under one owner, multiple radio stations under one chain, multiple cable networks under one parent. The economic drivers are well understood: scale economies in production, distribution, and back-office; portfolio effects in advertising sales (selling 30 stations to one advertiser is easier than selling each separately); cross-promotion across properties; and negotiating leverage with talent, sports leagues, and distributors.

The same dynamics drive vertical integration — owning content production, distribution, and exhibition. Hollywood's mid-20th-century studio system was vertically integrated until the 1948 Paramount antitrust decree forced divestiture of theatre chains. The cable-era reintegration combined content (studios), distribution (cable networks), and infrastructure (cable systems). Disney's 2019 acquisition of 21st Century Fox, AT&T's 2018 acquisition (later divestiture) of Time Warner, and Comcast's ownership of NBCUniversal illustrate the recurring pattern.

The regulatory response has been recurring antitrust intervention combined with sector-specific ownership rules. The classic FCC limits on broadcast ownership, the EU Merger Regulation framework, and the various national competition authorities have all intervened in media markets at various points. The political-economy pressure for stronger or weaker enforcement has shifted with administration, but the basic concern that media concentration affects democratic discourse — not just consumer welfare in the standard antitrust sense — has been a recurring theme in media policy for over a century.

concepts.title: The Major Conglomerates
concepts.contentHtml:
By the mid-2020s, the largest media conglomerates were a small set of Western and Asian giants. The Walt Disney Company — owner of the Disney studios, ABC, ESPN, the Marvel and Lucasfilm libraries, Pixar, Hulu, Disney+, the Disney parks and resorts — is roughly $90 billion in annual revenue. Comcast / NBCUniversal combines broadband infrastructure, the NBC broadcast and cable networks, Universal Pictures and theme parks, and the Peacock streaming service. Warner Bros. Discovery (formed 2022 from the WarnerMedia–Discovery merger) owns Warner Bros., HBO, CNN, the Discovery Channel, and many other properties.

The Murdoch empire, now reorganised across Fox Corporation (Fox News, Fox Sports, Fox Broadcasting) and News Corp (the Wall Street Journal, the New York Post, Times newspapers in the UK and Australia, HarperCollins), remains one of the most influential media holdings globally despite the 2019 sale of the entertainment-side Fox studios to Disney. Bertelsmann (Penguin Random House, RTL Group, Gruner + Jahr) is the dominant European media conglomerate. Sony, Paramount (Paramount Skydance since 2025), and the streaming-tech giants (Netflix, Amazon, Apple, Alphabet/Google, Meta) round out the top tier.

The contemporary picture is complicated by the tech platforms' role. Google and Meta are not classified as media companies in standard industry taxonomies but command roughly 60% of global digital ad revenue, exercising substantial influence on what content circulates and how publishers earn money. Amazon, Apple, and TikTok-parent ByteDance occupy similar tier. The traditional-media-versus-platform distinction increasingly fails to capture the actual economic structure of contemporary media markets, in which a handful of platforms intermediate the distribution of content produced by a much larger and more fragmented production layer.

concepts.title: Concentration, Diversity, and the Marketplace of Ideas
concepts.contentHtml:
The political-economy concern about media concentration has two distinct dimensions. The first is the economic: concentration produces market-power problems familiar to any antitrust analysis — higher prices, lower quality, reduced innovation. The second is the democratic: a small number of owners controlling a large share of news production may distort public discourse, suppress unwelcome stories, or simply reduce the diversity of perspectives available to citizens.

The empirical evidence is mixed. Studies including Matthew Gentzkow and Jesse Shapiro's work on US newspaper slant find that ownership matters less than one might expect — newspapers tend to align with reader preferences in their markets, and ownership effects are detectable but smaller than market-pull effects. Studies of Sinclair Broadcasting's centrally-distributed must-air editorials have found measurable but modest effects on local political coverage. The honest finding is that ownership concentration has detectable effects on coverage but the effects are smaller than the most polemical accounts suggest.

The contemporary version of the concentration debate has shifted toward platform power. The 2024 EU Digital Markets Act, the various US state and federal antitrust cases against Google and Meta, the UK CMA's interventions in digital advertising, and the Indian Competition Commission's actions all attempt to address the concentration of attention and revenue at the platform layer. Whether the resulting interventions produce a more pluralistic media ecosystem, or simply replace platform concentration with regulatory friction, is one of the central open questions of media-policy work.

title: Public vs Private Media
description: License fees, state grants, foundations, billionaire owners — funding tradeoffs

concepts.title: The Public-Service Broadcasting Model
concepts.contentHtml:
The public-service broadcasting (PSB) institutions of Western Europe, the Commonwealth, and Japan are among the most distinctive media organisations in the world. The BBC (UK, 1922 / 1927 charter), NHK (Japan, 1926), ARD and ZDF (Germany), RAI (Italy), the ABC (Australia), the CBC (Canada), and most of the Nordic broadcasters operate under formal charters, are funded primarily by household licence fees or hypothecated tax revenue, and are charged with serving citizens rather than just consumers.

The licence fee as a funding mechanism has political-economy advantages and disadvantages. Its main advantage is independence from advertiser pressure and (to a lesser extent) from year-to-year political pressure. Its main disadvantage is that it is essentially a regressive flat tax, justified largely by historical accident, and has become politically vulnerable as smaller cohorts of younger viewers consume primarily streaming content and resist paying for traditional broadcast. The BBC licence fee covers around £3.7 billion in 2024; debates about its continuation past the 2027 charter renewal have been intense.

The output of PSBs has historically set the news-quality benchmark in their countries even when they are not the most-watched outlets. BBC News, NHK, ARD's Tagesschau, ABC News in Australia — each commands a degree of public trust and reputation for accuracy that has been hard for purely commercial competitors to match. The institutional independence of these broadcasters from elected governments is a constant area of political contestation: charter renewals, board appointments, funding settlements, and legal-status changes are all moments when the model's independence is tested. The post-2020 period has seen multiple cases of pressure on PSBs (UK government appointments to the BBC Board; Hungarian and Polish ruling-party interventions in their public broadcasters; threats to NPR/PBS funding under the Trump administrations, culminating in the 2025 rescission of their federal funding).

concepts.title: State Media, State-Subsidised Media, and Editorial Independence
concepts.contentHtml:
The state-controlled media systems of many authoritarian and partially-authoritarian states sit at one end of a spectrum. RT (formerly Russia Today, founded 2005) and Sputnik; CGTN and Xinhua (China); Press TV (Iran); Saudi-owned Al-Arabiya; state media in Belarus, Hungary, Turkey, and many others serve their funding governments' messaging priorities directly. The line between these and PSBs in democracies can be ideologically contested, but the institutional differences in editorial independence, judicial protection, and journalist safety are large and well-documented.

The middle ground is a complex space. Al Jazeera (founded 1996, Qatari-funded) operates with substantial editorial independence within constraints set by the Qatari government's regional-policy interests. Voice of America, Radio Free Europe / Radio Liberty, the BBC World Service, Deutsche Welle, and France 24 are state-funded but operate under various legal frameworks intended to preserve editorial independence — the firewall between funder and editorial choices is a frequent topic of debate but generally substantively meaningful in practice.

The state-subsidy models for non-broadcast media are a separate set of arrangements. Nordic press subsidies — long-established direct support for newspapers below certain market positions — are the canonical example of a robust subsidy framework that has not produced obvious editorial dependence. Other models include the French aide à la presse, Italian contributi diretti, Canadian Local Journalism Initiative, and the various proposed US state-level local-journalism funds. Whether any of these can scale to substitute for the lost commercial-advertising revenue base is the central question of contemporary press-policy debates.

concepts.title: Foundations, Non-Profits, and Billionaire Owners
concepts.contentHtml:
Three further funding models have grown in importance through the digital era. The non-profit news sector — ProPublica (founded 2008, Sandler Foundation seed), The Marshall Project, Texas Tribune, The City, City Bureau, and an emerging US local-news non-profit network — combines foundation grants, individual donations, and limited commercial revenue. ProPublica's investigative work has produced multiple Pulitzer Prizes and has been formally recognised as a major institution in US journalism.

The foundation-grant ecosystem for journalism has expanded substantially. The MacArthur Foundation, Ford Foundation, Knight Foundation, Open Society Foundations, the Pew Charitable Trusts, and dozens of smaller funders provide grants for specific reporting projects, organisational sustainability, and cross-cutting initiatives. The European equivalent includes the Journalismfund Europe, the Reporters Shield initiative, and various national-level programs. The total foundation funding for US journalism reached over $400 million annually by the early 2020s — substantial but small compared to the lost advertising revenue it partially replaces.

The billionaire-owner model has produced both successes and failures. Jeff Bezos's 2013 acquisition of the Washington Post for $250 million was followed by a decade of growth in digital subscriptions, investment in newsroom expansion, and a return to profitability — until 2024–2025 when the publication faced renewed political and editorial pressure that has tested the model. Marc Benioff's purchase of Time, Patrick Soon-Shiong's purchase of the Los Angeles Times, Laurene Powell Jobs's purchase of the Atlantic, and others have produced mixed results. The model is fundamentally vulnerable to the owner's continuing willingness to subsidise; it is not a long-run substitute for an underlying business model that pays for itself.

title: The Platform Economy
description: Google, Meta, TikTok — how aggregators captured the ad market

concepts.title: How Google and Meta Captured Digital Advertising
concepts.contentHtml:
The contemporary digital advertising market is dominated by two companies. Google (Alphabet) and Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp) together account for roughly 60% of global digital ad revenue. The combined revenue of these two companies' advertising businesses exceeded $400 billion in 2024 — more than the entire global newspaper industry's peak revenue at any point in history.

The economic mechanism behind the duopoly's dominance is the combination of three advantages. The first is data scale: Google's search-query data and Meta's social-graph and behavioural data give them targeting precision that smaller publishers cannot match. The second is auction efficiency: real-time bidding and continuous optimisation across billions of impressions per day produces better matches between advertiser preferences and ad inventory than slower negotiated processes. The third is self-serve simplicity: Google Ads and Meta Ads Manager allow any small business to run targeted campaigns with budgets as low as a few dollars, expanding the advertiser base far beyond what traditional media sales operations could reach.

The publisher economics of this transformation have been brutal. The same advertiser dollar that previously flowed to a local newspaper or magazine now flows to platforms whose marginal cost of serving each impression is essentially zero. Google's Ad Tech stack (DoubleClick, AdSense, AdMob, AdX) intermediates much of the rest of the digital ad market, taking margins at multiple layers between advertisers and publishers. The 2023 US Department of Justice and EU antitrust cases against Google's ad-tech business specifically targeted these intermediation margins. Whether structural remedies emerge from these cases is one of the central open questions of late-decade competition policy.

concepts.title: Platform–Publisher Tensions
concepts.contentHtml:
The platform-publisher relationship has been one of the most difficult negotiations of the digital era. Publishers depend on platforms for traffic but resent the share of revenue platforms capture; platforms depend on publishers for content but resist sharing audience data or revenue at the levels publishers demand. The relationship has produced several distinct conflict patterns.

The Australian News Media Bargaining Code (2021) was the first major regulatory intervention requiring platforms to negotiate with news publishers over content compensation. After Meta briefly blocked news content from Australian Facebook in protest, both Google and Meta reached commercial agreements with major Australian publishers. The model has been imitated and modified in Canada (Online News Act, 2023, which produced Meta's still-current news block in that country), France (under the EU Copyright Directive's neighbouring rights), Germany, and elsewhere. The intellectual case against the model — that it amounts to a tax on linking and produces predictable platform-side responses — has been argued by Cory Doctorow and others.

The traffic referral patterns have shifted dramatically. Facebook's policy changes (the 2018 News Feed changes that demoted news, the 2024 reduction of news visibility further) cut publisher traffic from Meta substantially. Google's AI Overviews (introduced 2024) and the broader trend toward AI-summarised search results threaten to reduce search-driven traffic to publishers further. The publishers' increasing dependence on direct subscriber relationships — newsletters, apps, podcast distribution — partly reflects strategic adaptation to a platform environment where any single platform can change the rules at any time.

concepts.title: TikTok, Amazon, and the Diversification of Platform Power
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-2020 period has seen the platform-economy concentrate further along certain dimensions while diversifying along others. TikTok's rise as the dominant attention destination among under-25s has changed the calculus for advertisers and publishers alike. The platform's For You Page algorithmic distribution made viral reach available to creators without traditional follower bases, and its full-screen vertical-video format has shaped product design across competing platforms. By 2024 its parent ByteDance (including China's Douyin) captured an estimated 10–15% share of global digital ad revenue.

Amazon's advertising business has grown rapidly into a third major player alongside Google and Meta. The combination of search advertising on Amazon.com (high-intent purchase queries that monetise more effectively than nearly any other ad surface) with Amazon Prime Video advertising (rolled out 2024), Twitch advertising, and the broader Amazon DSP (demand-side platform) gave Amazon over $50 billion in 2024 ad revenue — a new entrant from a different starting point. Apple Search Ads in the App Store, Microsoft's Bing/Edge advertising, and X's diminished but still-meaningful ad business round out the major commercial platform-side players.

The aggregate effect on the media economy is mixed. Total advertising revenue has grown — global ad spending crossed $1 trillion in 2024 for the first time — but the share captured by platforms versus traditional publishers has continued shifting toward platforms. The publisher response, focused on direct-subscriber relationships and diversified revenue streams, has produced both strong national winners and a continuing crisis at the local-news level. Whether the regulatory interventions (DSA, DMA, ad-tech antitrust cases, news-media bargaining codes) substantially reshape the underlying economics is the central question of media-policy work for the next several years.
